description: A caravan desert. Salt pans, saguaro scrub and days between wells; water and salt are the currency and everybody talks about the road.

appearance.water-seller: A skin under each arm and a tin cup on a string, and he has counted both.
appearance.saltman: Hands cracked white to the wrist, which he no longer notices.
appearance.glassblower: Eyebrows gone, and a squint that does not come off between jobs.
appearance.caravan-master: Doing sums about you before the greeting is finished.
appearance.muleteer: Smells of animal, dust and animal. Talks to you over his shoulder.
appearance.date-farmer: Up a ladder somewhere in the shade, and staying there.
appearance.well-keeper: Sat with his back to the shaft, in the only cold place for a day's ride.
appearance.headman: Old, still, and the only person here not doing something.
appearance.reader: Following a line with one finger and losing it whenever you speak.
appearance.drover: Smells of the road and of somebody else's animals.
appearance.weaver: At the loom, in the dark, because the dark is where it is cool.

talksAbout.water-seller: the price this week, and who is watering short
talksAbout.well-keeper: the level in the shaft, and what it was at this time last year
talksAbout.caravan-master: the road east, what it costs, and who is not coming back on it
talksAbout.saltman: the pans, the season, and the weight that is lost in carriage
talksAbout.headman: the wells, the road tax, and who has stopped paying it
talksAbout.muleteer: the animals, the flies, and the last three waystations

lore.title: The Dry Season
lore.premise: Two of the four wells on the eastern road have gone brackish in one season, and the caravans have started taking a longer way that nobody has surveyed. The waystations between are still expecting them.
lore.era: the eleventh year of the long drought
deities: the One Who Counts the Days

ambient: The heat comes up off the ground as much as down onto it.
Something has been dragged across the road here, and the wind is halfway through hiding it.
A saguaro throws the only shade for a hundred paces, and it is the wrong shape to sit in.
The air over the pan is moving in a way that is not wind.
Nothing has walked this stretch since the last time it blew.

warehouse: Cut square, and heavier than it looks.
Wrapped twice, and it has stained the wrapping.
shop: A string of them, blue, against the eye.
In a block, wrapped in leaf.
stable: Repaired more often than it was made.
inn: Filled here, and they watched you watch them do it.
Cooked on the stones an hour ago.
house: Sweating, which is how it works.
Tight enough to hold water, and it has.
hall: Notched for every caravan through, and the notches stop.
For lamps, and rationed like everything else.
ruin: Struck by a house that no longer exists.
Empty a long time. Somebody kept it anyway.
smithy: A sack of it, light as nothing.

shop: Two days of it, if you are honest with yourself.
Sold by weight, and the weight is the argument.
Sweet enough to make you thirsty, which is the trade.
Blue, against the eye. Everybody wears one.
Undyed. The dyed ones cost twice and burn the same.
Dented, but the shutter still works.
smithy: For getting a bucket back out of a shaft.
Flat-toned, so it carries over sand.
Second-hand. Somebody's initials are on the pommel.
stable: Repaired more often than it was made.
Enough for a week on the road.
Faded to no colour at all.
inn: Cooked on the stones an hour ago.
Poured from a height, for no reason anybody will explain.
A roof, a mat, and the animals audible all night.
warehouse: Sold by the bale and stolen by the handful.

bush: Edible under duress, which the road provides.
saguaro: Cloudy, and it will keep you upright for an afternoon.
Split it and it is better than it looks.
palm: Astringent, and they will be better in a month.
Twists into cord if you have the evening.
rock: It takes a hard edge and a harder spark.
Prised off in a sheet, and it tastes of the ground.
gravel: Swept up where the pan has dried and dried again.
marsh: The pale ends, which are worth the wet feet.
Sodden, and it holds far more water than it looks able to.
deadTree: Split from a trunk that has been dead longer than the road.
